passage:
Playschool note, Tuesday
At circle time, Jatin, 5, told us he saw a green monster behind the slide at the park, "with three eyes and a long tail". He wasn't joking; he looked worried.
Later I read our storybook. Its monster has three eyes and a long tail. Jatin pointed. "That's the one I saw!"
He remembers the monster clearly but has mixed up the book with the park.
I told him, "That monster lives in the book. Let's check the park together." We peeped behind the slide and found a green watering can. He laughed.
Amandeep

qa.q: What was really behind the slide?
qa.a: A green watering can was behind the slide.

qa.q: Why did Jatin look worried at circle time?
qa.a: He truly believed he had seen the monster at the park, because he remembered it clearly but had lost track that it came from the storybook.

qa.q: What did Amandeep do to help Jatin, and why is it gentle?
qa.a: Amandeep said the monster lives in the book and checked behind the slide with Jatin, so he could see for himself without being called a liar.

qa.q: How might the other children at circle time feel hearing about the monster?
qa.a: Some might feel scared of the park, so checking it together could help them feel safe too.

grounding: It shows a preschool boy who says he saw a monster at the park when it came from a storybook.

passage:
In the village, Selvam, four, ran home from the play area under the banyan tree. "Amma! A ghost in a white sheet was near the swing!"
Kavitha put down the rice winnow. "Where?"
"Near the swing. It went whooo."
She remembered that their neighbour Ayesha akka had told the children a ghost story the night before, with a white sheet.
Kavitha took his hand and walked to the banyan tree. A white cloth was drying on the fence, flapping in the wind.
"Is this your ghost?" she asked. Selvam stared, then giggled. "Ayesha akka's ghost is in her story."

qa.q: What was flapping on the fence near the banyan tree?
qa.a: A white cloth was drying on the fence, flapping in the wind.

qa.q: Why did Selvam believe the ghost was near the swing?
qa.a: Ayesha akka's story with the white sheet stayed in his head, and he lost track that it came from the story, not the play area.

qa.q: What did Kavitha choose to do instead of dismissing him?
qa.a: She took his hand and walked to the banyan tree with him, so he could see the cloth and sort out the story from what was real.

qa.q: How might Ayesha akka feel if she heard about the ghost?
qa.a: She might smile, or decide to tell gentler stories, since her ghost followed Selvam all the way to the swing.

grounding: It shows a preschool boy who reports seeing a ghost at the play area when it came from a story he heard.

passage:
On Monday in Berlin, five-year-old Adam told his kindergarten teacher, Selin, "I saw a dragon in the park yesterday! It was sleeping under the bridge."
Selin asked, "What did it look like?"
"Blue with gold spots. It snored."
At pickup, Selin told his mother, Nour, who smiled. "On Saturday we read a book about a blue dragon under a bridge. On Sunday we walked past the park bridge."
At home Nour opened the book. Adam pointed. "That's my dragon!" Then: "But I saw it at the park."
"You saw the bridge at the park," Nour said. "The dragon lives in this book."

qa.q: Where did Adam say the dragon was sleeping?
qa.a: Adam said it was sleeping under the bridge in the park.

qa.q: Why does Adam still say, "But I saw it at the park"?
qa.a: He remembers the dragon vividly and really did see the park bridge, so the story and the walk have blended and he has lost track of where the dragon came from.

qa.q: How did Nour help Adam untangle the memory?
qa.a: She showed him the book and calmly said he saw the bridge at the park while the dragon lives in the book.

qa.q: Why was it useful that Selin asked what the dragon looked like instead of saying it wasn't real?
qa.a: Selin's open question let Adam share the details, which later helped Nour link them to the book without making him feel foolish.

grounding: It shows a preschool boy who says he saw a dragon in the park when it came from a picture book.

passage: At the city library's children's corner, Gargi, the librarian, asked what everyone did at the weekend. Chirag, five, shot up his hand. "I saw a monster in the park! A purple one with spiky hair, and it ate the swings!" Neelam, the helper, caught Gargi's eye. On Friday she had read them a picture book about a purple monster who ate a playground. Gargi didn't laugh. "Chirag, where did you meet it: in the park, or in a book?" "In the park." Then his eyes found the purple cover on the shelf. "Ohh. That one." He grinned. "It was in the park in the book."

qa.q: What did Chirag say the monster ate?
qa.a: It ate the swings.

qa.q: Why was Chirag so sure he met the monster in the park?
qa.a: He remembered the monster and the park clearly but had lost track that both came from the picture book, so it felt like something he saw.

qa.q: How did Gargi help Chirag find where the monster came from?
qa.a: Gargi didn't laugh and asked a gentle either-or question, park or book, which gave him space to notice the cover and sort it out himself.

qa.q: Why did Neelam catch Gargi's eye when Chirag spoke?
qa.a: Neelam recognised the monster from the book she read on Friday and wanted Gargi to know the story's real source.

grounding: A preschool boy reports seeing a monster in the park that actually came from a picture book, having lost track of the source.

passage: I'm Harish, Ojas's big brother. On Sunday night Dadi told us about the hairy monster that lives in the old tamarind tree. Ojas, five, listened with the blanket up to his nose. On Tuesday we went to the colony park, and he just played on the slide. But yesterday he told his nursery class, "I saw a hairy monster in the tamarind tree at the park! It waved at me!" His teacher phoned Mummy. I don't think he was fibbing; he told it the way he tells about the slide. He knows the monster well. He just forgot it came from Dadi's story, not the park.

qa.q: Where did Dadi say the hairy monster lives?
qa.a: In the old tamarind tree.

qa.q: Why did Ojas tell the class about the monster so confidently?
qa.a: He knew the monster well from Dadi's story and had lost track of where it came from, so to him it felt like something seen at the park.

qa.q: What could Mummy ask Ojas to help sort out the story?
qa.a: She could gently ask, "Did you see it at the park, or hear about it from Dadi?", letting him find the source without calling it a lie.

qa.q: How might Ojas's teacher have felt hearing about the monster?
qa.a: The teacher was probably puzzled and a little concerned, unsure whether something had really frightened him at the park.

grounding: An older brother notices his preschool brother telling a grandmother's monster story as something he saw at the park.

passage:
Kindergarten note, Monday.
Mridul came in this morning bursting with news: "I saw a dragon in the park! It had green wings and it lived under the slide!" He was completely serious. Chinmay said his older brother had told them a dragon story on Saturday, sitting on that slide. I asked Mridul gently, "Did you see it with your eyes, or did you hear about it?" He thought hard. "I saw it... in the story." Then, a minute later: "But it was under the slide!" He wasn't fibbing; he knew the dragon, just not where it came from. We drew the dragon together and wrote 'from Chinmay's brother's story' at the bottom.

qa.q: Where did Mridul say the dragon lived?
qa.a: Under the slide.

qa.q: Why was Mridul so sure he saw a dragon?
qa.a: Mridul felt excited and certain, because the story heard on the slide stayed in his mind but he had lost track that it was only a story.

qa.q: What did the teacher do, and why is it a gentle way to help?
qa.a: The teacher asked whether he saw it or heard it, and they drew the dragon labelled with where it came from, helping him sort the source without calling it a lie.

qa.q: How might Chinmay feel about Mridul's dragon news?
qa.a: Chinmay might feel amused, knowing the dragon came from his brother's story.

grounding: Shows a preschooler sure he saw a dragon at the park when it came from a story he heard there.

passage: In the village of Mandwa, Nitin, four, ran into the kitchen shouting, "Aai! I saw a tiger in the sugarcane! A big one, with stripes!" Payal put down the rolling pin. There were no tigers anywhere near Mandwa. "When did you see it?" "Yesterday! It was hiding and it roared!" Payal thought. Last night Ajoba had told him a bedtime story about a tiger in a sugarcane field, roaring at a farmer. "Did Ajoba tell you a tiger story?" Nitin nodded eagerly. "Yes! The tiger in the sugarcane!" Then he frowned, puzzled. The tiger was so real in his head that he couldn't tell where he had met it.

qa.q: Who told Nitin the bedtime story?
qa.a: Ajoba told him the bedtime story.

qa.q: Why did Nitin frown at the end?
qa.a: Nitin felt puzzled, because the tiger felt so real that he couldn't tell whether he had seen it or only heard about it.

qa.q: How did Payal help sort out the tiger story?
qa.a: She asked when he saw it and whether Ajoba had told a tiger story, gently linking the tiger to its real source.

qa.q: How might Ajoba feel if he heard about the tiger sighting?
qa.a: Ajoba would probably feel amused and touched that his story felt so real to Nitin.

grounding: Shows a preschooler sure he saw a tiger in the fields when it came from a bedtime story.

passage: Paulo, five, came home from the club in São Paulo and told his father, Mateo, "There was a shark in the big pool! It swam right past my feet!" Mateo had been at the pool the whole time and seen only a few inflatable rings. "What colour?" "Grey, with big teeth!" That morning, Paulo had watched a cartoon where a shark leapt out of a swimming pool. Mateo smiled. "Did you see it in the cartoon, or at the club?" Paulo opened his mouth, then closed it. "Both?" he tried. He wasn't lying. The shark was real to him; only its source had slipped away.

qa.q: What did Mateo see at the pool?
qa.a: Only a few inflatable rings.

qa.q: Why did Paulo say 'Both?'
qa.a: Paulo felt unsure and a little confused, because the cartoon shark felt real but he couldn't remember where he had met it.

qa.q: What question did Mateo ask, and why is it helpful?
qa.a: 'Did you see it in the cartoon, or at the club?', which helps Paulo think about where the memory came from without calling him a liar.

qa.q: How might Mateo feel hearing about the shark?
qa.a: Mateo probably felt amused and understanding, having been at the pool the whole time.

grounding: Shows a preschooler describing a shark at the pool that actually came from a cartoon he watched.

passage:
It was Children's Day at the kindergarten, and the classroom was full of paper flags. Vikas, five, raised his hand at circle time.

"I saw a green monster in the park! With three eyes!"

The children gasped. His teacher Gargi asked, "Where did you see it?"

"At the park. Near the swings."

"Was it maybe in a story?"

Vikas thought hard. "Papa read me a book. The monster was in the park in the book."

"So you heard about it in a story?"

"Yes. But it was at the park." He nodded, very sure.

qa.q: Where did Vikas say he saw the monster?
qa.a: At the park, near the swings.

qa.q: Why was Vikas so sure about the monster?
qa.a: He felt excited and certain, because he remembered the monster clearly but had lost track that it came from a book.

qa.q: How did Gargi help Vikas think about where the monster came from?
qa.a: She gently asked where he saw it and whether it was in a story, helping Vikas think about the source without scolding.

qa.q: How might the other children feel hearing about the monster?
qa.a: They were probably excited and a bit scared, which is why they gasped.

grounding: A preschooler says he saw a monster at the park when it came from a story he heard; he's lost track of the source.

passage:
Sunday, during Pongal. Ujjwal's grandmother Vidya told him a story about a crocodile that lived in the temple tank long ago.

Tuesday. Ujjwal, four, told his friends, "There's a crocodile in the temple tank! I saw it!"

Thursday. At the temple, Ujjwal hid behind Vidya's sari. "Paati, the crocodile."

Vidya knelt. "Where did you see it?"

"In the tank."

"Or in Paati's story?"

Ujjwal thought, frowning. "Your story."

"The story is from long ago. Look, just fish now."

He peeked. Fish swam by, and he laughed.

qa.q: What did Vidya's story say lived in the temple tank?
qa.a: A crocodile that lived in the temple tank long ago.

qa.q: Why did Ujjwal hide behind Vidya's sari?
qa.a: He felt scared, because he had lost track that the crocodile came from a story and thought it was real.

qa.q: What did Vidya do that helped Ujjwal?
qa.a: She asked where he saw it, helped him remember it was her story, and showed him the fish.

qa.q: How might Ujjwal's friends have felt when he told them about the crocodile?
qa.a: They were probably excited or scared, believing there was a crocodile in the tank.

grounding: A preschooler says he saw a crocodile when it was a story he heard, losing track of where it came from.

passage:
Snow had closed the hill school for the week, and the power was out in Chinmay's house in Shimla. By lamplight, Chinmay, five, told his sister Devika, "I saw a bear in the garden yesterday!"

Devika frowned. "We were inside all day."

"I saw it. A big black bear."

"Chinmay, remember Papa told us about the bear he saw as a boy?"

Chinmay was quiet. "The bear with the honey?"

"Yes. That's Papa's bear."

"But I saw it," he said, less sure now.

Devika gave him a hug. "It's a good bear story anyway."

qa.q: Where did Chinmay say he saw the bear?
qa.a: In the garden yesterday.

qa.q: Why did Chinmay become less sure?
qa.a: He felt confused, because he remembered the bear but not that it came from Papa's story.

qa.q: Which choice by Devika helped Chinmay, and why?
qa.a: Reminding Chinmay kindly that it was Papa's bear, and hugging him instead of calling him a liar, helped him feel safe while he rethought it.

qa.q: How might Devika feel when Chinmay insists he saw the bear?
qa.a: Devika may feel amused and patient, understanding that he isn't lying.

grounding: A preschooler says he saw a bear when it was a story he heard; he knows the content but lost track of the source.

passage: During Ganpati week, the colony park in Thane was full of lights and dhol practice. At dinner, Vijay announced, "I saw a monster in the park! It had green hair and lived inside the slide." Aai smiled. "When?" "Today!" Vijay's friend Imran, visiting with his mother, giggled. "That's from the book Miss read us! The slide monster!" Vijay frowned. He knew the monster so well: its green hair, its sleepy yawn. But had he seen it, or heard it? "I saw it in my head," he decided, and went back to his puri.

qa.q: Where did Vijay say the monster lived?
qa.a: Inside the slide.

qa.q: Why does Vijay frown when Imran mentions the book?
qa.a: He feels puzzled, because he knows the monster's green hair and yawn so well that it feels seen, but he has lost track of where it came from.

qa.q: How could Aai help Vijay sort story from real?
qa.a: Ask gently, "Did you see it, or hear it in a story?" and praise him for remembering the story so well.

qa.q: What is it like for Imran when Vijay claims the monster?
qa.a: Imran finds it funny and is happy to point to the book, since he remembers exactly where the monster came from.

grounding: A preschooler reports seeing a monster in the park that actually came from a story he heard.

"Papa, there was a tiger at the fair! A big one, with a gold crown!"
"At the Lohri fair? A real tiger, Vikas?"
"Yes! It roared at the bonfire!"
Farhan looked up from his peanuts. "Tigers don't wear crowns."
"This one did. I saw it."
"Where was it standing?" Papa asked.
"Near... um... in the jungle part."
"There's no jungle at the fair, beta," Papa said kindly. "Is it the tiger king from Dadi's bedtime story last night?"
Vikas stopped. His eyes went wide. "The tiger king! He roars at the fire in the story!"
"So you heard it," Farhan said.
"I heard it," Vikas agreed, "but it felt like seeing."

qa.q: What did Vikas say the tiger was wearing?
qa.a: A gold crown.

qa.q: What does Vikas's wide-eyed surprise suggest?
qa.a: His eyes went wide with surprise when he linked it to Dadi's story; he truly felt he had seen it and seemed amazed to find the real source.

qa.q: What made Papa's response helpful?
qa.a: He asked calmly where the tiger stood and linked it to Dadi's story, instead of calling Vikas a liar.

qa.q: How does Farhan see the tiger story?
qa.a: Farhan is doubtful, since tigers don't wear crowns, and seems satisfied once the story source is found.

grounding: A preschooler says he saw a crowned tiger at the fair, but it came from a bedtime story he heard.

passage: Teacher's note, first week of the monsoon. Gautam told the class that a crocodile lives in the big puddle in the park near his building. He described its yellow eyes and "snappy teeth" and was upset when Gargi said, "No, it doesn't." I remembered we had read the crocodile-in-the-drain story on Monday. I asked, "Where did you first meet the crocodile, Gautam?" He thought for a long time and said, "In the book?" I told him that was clever remembering. I have asked his father to talk about "seen" and "heard" at home.

qa.q: What story had the class read on Monday?
qa.a: The crocodile-in-the-drain story.

qa.q: Why was Gautam upset when Gargi disagreed?
qa.a: He felt sure and a bit hurt, because the yellow eyes and teeth felt like something he had seen; he had lost track that it came from a book.

qa.q: How did the teacher help Gautam?
qa.a: By asking an open question about where he first met the crocodile, praising his remembering, and asking his father to practise "seen" and "heard" at home.

qa.q: How might Gargi feel during the argument?
qa.a: Gargi may feel frustrated or confused that Gautam insists on something Gargi knows is not there.

grounding: A preschooler reports a crocodile in the park that he actually met in a class story.

passage:
On Holi evening in the village, Tushar ran to Aai, eyes huge. "I saw a big monster at the playground! It had three eyes and lived under the slide!"
His cousin Manoj burst out laughing. "That's my story! I told you that last night at bedtime."
"No, I SAW it," Tushar insisted, stamping his coloured feet. "Under the slide."
Aai pulled him close. "Did you see it with your eyes, or hear it in Manoj Dada's story?"
Tushar frowned hard, thinking. "I... don't know."

qa.q: Where did Tushar say the monster lived?
qa.a: Under the slide.

qa.q: Why does Tushar insist he saw the monster?
qa.a: He remembers the monster clearly but has lost track that it came from Manoj Dada's story, so he feels sure and a little scared.

qa.q: Why was Aai's question a good one?
qa.a: It gently asked where the monster came from without calling Tushar a liar, helping him notice he might have heard it in a story.

qa.q: How does Manoj see Tushar's monster?
qa.a: Manoj finds it funny, because he recognises it as his own bedtime story.

grounding: Shows a preschooler who says he saw a monster when it came from a story he heard.
